rss.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
rss.summary: How $1,500 could qualify every company in the world, why customers hate the model selector, and how Clay is building go-to-market infrastructure for every agent
rss.text_excerpt:
Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue , the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation . By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. rss.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
rss.summary: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. Tags: backups , sqlite

rss.summary: My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News. I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that. He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted. The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too! Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously. (Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.) rss.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
rss.summary: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I'm getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it . That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand. rss.title: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability.
rss.summary: Google launches Humanity’s First Exam to test LLM reliability across 544 prompts.
rss.text_excerpt: Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings. Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE. Explore the live leaderboard , or read our technical report . To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week Kaggle competition through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong. Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue)

rss.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
rss.summary: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

rss.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
rss.summary: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
rss.text_excerpt:
Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. Then your coding agent writes the code from the approved prompts and proves the real user path with `pdd prove`. ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Prompt
the source"] --> S["Story
what a person can do"] S --> L["Lint & Test
pdd lint · pdd test"] L --> T["Run Prompt
pdd PROMPT.md"] T --> A["Review & Approve

code · pdd prove"] ``` PDD is the `pdd` command and one `/pdd` skill (`$pdd` in Codex, `/pdd` in Claude Code) with on-demand references for your coding agent. In interactive workflows, you approve changed prompts in chat or GitHub PR review and authorize pull requests. # `Anda` > A Rust framework for building composable AI agent runtimes. ## README Translations [English readme](./README.md) | [中文说明](./README_CN.md) | [日本語の説明](./README_JA.md) ## Introduction Anda is a Rust framework for building AI agents that can combine models, tools, memory, and other agents into a single runtime. It focuses on composability, type-safe extension points, asynchronous execution, and practical runtime control. The core engine lets developers register agents and tools, route model requests by capability labels, call local or remote functions, isolate context state, and add optional persistence or memory layers when an application needs them. ![Anda Diagram](./anda_diagram.webp) ## Key Features 1. **Composable agents and tools** Agents and tools are registered through stable traits and function definitions, so specialized components can be combined into larger workflows without hard-coding one application shape. 2. **Model routing** The engine can route completion requests through labeled model tiers such as `primary`, `pro`, `flash`, or `lite`, while provider-specific adapters stay behind a common request and output contract. 3. **Runtime orchestration** `CompletionRunner` handles iterative model turns, tool calls, agent calls, usage accounting, artifacts, steering messages, follow-up messages, cancellation, and compact continuation handoffs for long-running sessions, which the model can also trigger itself at a task boundary with a handoff it writes. Subagents add root-scoped identity, turn-completion events, bounded messaging and shared budgets, with opt-in idle checkpoints and explicit context handoffs. See [subagent lifecycle](./docs/subagents.md). 4. **Scoped execution context** `BaseCtx` and `AgentCtx` provide isolated state, cache, object storage, HTTP calls, signed calls, cancellation, and child contexts for each agent or tool. 5. **Extensible memory and skills** Optional extensions provide conversation storage, KIP-based memory tools, filesystem access, shell execution, fetch, notes, todos, and file-backed skills. Coding agents can opt into a shell/session/patch bundle with bounded output, supervised processes, and optional macOS/Linux process sandboxing; restricted file agents can register filesystem tools without granting shell access. github.description: A durable agent harness: sessions that survive a crash or kill -9, approvals that persist, background tasks, sessions that start and message each other (preview), any model. A 2,200-line TypeScript kernel, with a coding agent for the terminal and the browser built on it.
github.text_excerpt:
### A durable agent harness that picks up where it left off. **In your terminal or your browser. Any model you have. A `kill -9` costs you nothing.**
A TypeScript kernel capped at 2,200 lines, and a coding agent built on it. v0.56.2 · Node ≥ 22 · macOS and Linux [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@vincemakes/kiso-code?label=npm&color=111111)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@vincemakes/kiso-code) [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/vincemakes/kiso/ci.yml?branch=main&label=CI&color=111111)](https://github.com/vincemakes/kiso/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-111111)](LICENSE) ![macOS](https://img.shields.io/badge/macOS-000000?logo=apple&logoColor=white) ![Linux](https://img.shields.io/badge/Linux-000000?logo=linux&logoColor=white) **[Install](#quick-start)** · **[kiso web](#kiso-web)** · **[Docs](#documentation)** · **[kiso.work](https://kiso.work)** · **English** · [简体中文](README.zh.md)

## Is kiso for you? - **You switch models.** DeepSeek, Claude, GPT, a ChatGPT subscription, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint or gateway, with the effort level each one accepts. - **Your tasks are long, and things die.** A crash, a `kill -9`, a closed laptop: `kiso resume` continues from what was committed. A command whose outcome is unknown goes to you, never silently repeated. - **You want to see where it goes.** Every turn ends with its input, output, cache hits and speed; every session is a JSONL log you can read. - **You build agents yourself.** The harness is a library: a durable session store, an agent factory and a typed event stream. If you want a cloud agent that works while your machine is off, or Windows today, kiso is not that yet. ## Terminal or browser: one agent

github.text_excerpt: # Yardlet [![CI](https://github.com/zzunkie/yardlet/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/zzunkie/yardlet/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/zzunkie/yardlet?label=release)](https://github.com/zzunkie/yardlet/releases/latest) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/github/license/zzunkie/yardlet)](LICENSE) [![macOS 15+](https://img.shields.io/badge/macOS-15%2B-000000?logo=apple&logoColor=white)](#requirements) Lightweight, non-intrusive, yet versatile ADE. Yardlet is a native macOS app that runs the real agent CLIs you already use, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity CLI and others, side by side in one window of projects and tasks, each with the agent loop, sign-in and session history it already has. By default it adds no agent layer of its own: no hooks, no wrappers around the agent commands, and nothing written into the agents' settings. The few options that go further are off until you turn them on (see [Off by default](#off-by-default)). Yardlet is written in Swift and SwiftUI; it is not a web view. It uses 53 MiB of memory at rest after a first launch and 214 MiB with ten tasks streaming at once, not counting the agents' own CLIs (Yardlet 0.11.10 on an M1 Pro MacBook Pro with macOS 15.6, November 2026). It does not replace the agents or proxy their accounts: it starts the CLI you already use, with the account you already signed in to. Most of us will end up with an agent workbench of our own.
